extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in mathematics; maths students and teachers
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating or producing mathematical solutions and explanations with attention to aesthetic qualities (elegance, clarity, insight) and to pedagogical choices that help others appreciate mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance of approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer an approach that 'seems most elegant' — when faced with several strategies, choose the one that appears most elegant first; revisit solutions that seem clumsy to try to make them more attractive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author uses this as a guiding heuristic when solving problems: elegance motivates study and guides strategy choice. Example: between two correct student solutions, the author prefers the one that captures the essence rather than the longer, cluttered one. If a solution seems clumsy, revisit it to simplify or improve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveals the 'why' (explanatory depth)
rubrics_metrics.description: A beautiful mathematical argument 'helps the reader to understand why this piece of mathematics works this way, not just that it does.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuable solutions expose the underlying ideas and mechanisms. Example: the triangular-number proof that pairs two triangles into a rectangle shows why the formula (n(n+1)/2) holds, not just that it does. This explanatory quality is 'critical' for mathematicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy / parsimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that avoid unnecessary clutter and distractions; an economy to the argument such that a single diagram or idea captures everything needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author contrasts a longer, cluttered solution with one that is economical. Example: the dots-and-rectangle diagram 'painlessly generalises' and a 'single diagram captures everything we need to know.' Economy contributes to memorability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalisability
rubrics_metrics.description: A beautiful argument generalises neatly to broader cases (e.g., from the 10th triangular number to the 1000th) rather than applying only to a single instance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dots-duplication argument generalises from any n to the formula n(n+1)/2; generalisability is praised as part of the argument's power and elegance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of the argument
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument's ability to 'tame' difficult concepts (such as infinity) with a simple, convincing idea is part of its beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: grouping terms of the harmonic series so each group exceeds 1/2 provides a powerful, elegant proof of divergence. The combination of persuasive simplicity and conceptual control is valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memorability / vividness
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanations that are memorable — easy to recall and that stick with the learner — are aesthetically appealing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dots diagram is described as a 'memorable explanation' compared to a formula-guessing/induction approach which may prove correctness but not provide the same memorable insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of visual / diagrammatic reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagrams or pictures that capture the idea succinctly (e.g., dots forming triangles and rectangles) are an effective route to beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author highlights drawing dots, duplicating and rotating to make a rectangle as an example of a beautiful, pictorial argument. Visual reasoning can convey the essence in one image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual (insightful) vs mechanical proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptual proofs that expose reasons and structure are preferred over procedural or purely mechanical proofs that only verify results (e.g., a guessed formula proved by induction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author contrasts deriving a formula by noticing first terms and proving by induction (mechanical) with the pictorial argument (conceptual) that 'conveys the same memorable explanation behind the formula.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Solutions should be well explained and accessible; clarity in explanation matters for appreciation and understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although both student solutions referenced were 'described well,' clarity alone is not sufficient for beauty — clarity combined with insight and economy is ideal. Clear exposition supports the learner's ability to perceive the beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requires comprehension to appreciate
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic appreciation of mathematics often requires grappling with terminology, notation and ideas; one may need to persevere before perceiving beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes that she 'cannot find a piece of mathematics beautiful unless I first understand it properly' and that this process can take time, similar to appreciating complex art or music.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical conditions that foster appreciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching and learning practices that give students opportunities to experience mathematical beauty: engage with rich questions, play with ideas, and encounter multiple strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recommends giving students rich tasks, opportunities to play with mathematical ideas, and presenting multiple strategies rather than only answers. These practices deepen understanding and enable appreciation of aesthetic qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate problem selection for learners
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist beautiful mathematical problems that are accessible to school students; selecting such problems can enable early encounters with mathematical beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes that mathematical ideas 'do not have to be university level' to be beautiful and praises teachers and projects that help students have experiences of mathematical beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison between solutions as an evaluative tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparing two different correct solutions can reveal aesthetic differences — e.g., one may capture essence and the other may be longer or contain unnecessary steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author illustrates this by comparing two students' correct solutions and preferring the one that captures the essence. Comparison helps highlight economy, insight, and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as a heuristic in problem-solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic judgement (finding a solution beautiful) can function as a heuristic guide in choosing strategies when working on problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author states that enjoyment of beauty 'is part of what motivates me to study the subject' and that it serves as a guide when working on a problem: choose strategies that seem elegant first.
